title: Access-Intent Query Gate and Credential Cache for Usage Analytics
creator: Maya Chen
description: Add a lightweight access-intent evaluation layer at the analytics API edge and a short-lived credentials cache to speed permission checks for usage and cost views. The goal is to enforce per-dataset and per-row visibility predicates without adding >10ms median latency for common queries, and to provide auditable links between request tokens and dataset access decisions.
background: Current analytics endpoints perform full authorization lookups inside the query execution path, which hits the permissions mapper and entitlements store per request. This produces variable latency on high-cardinality workloads and increases DB pressure during peak dashboards. We have existing work on a permissions mapper and scoped delegation (see parent ENG-24109) but we lack an edge cache/evaluator that can be used by the query router to do fast query rewriting and to attach audit metadata.
proposal: Implement an Access-Intent Query Gate service that: (1) accepts request context (token, route, dataset_id, requested_aggregation) and returns an 'effective visibility predicate' (SQL snippet or canonical predicate token) plus an audit reference; (2) keeps a credentials cache keyed by (principal_id, dataset_id, role_hash) with TTL and invalidation hooks; (3) integrates with the analytics query router to inject visibility predicates before the planner stage; and (4) emits an audit event tying request->decision for downstream retention in audit logs.
design_decisions: Centralized gate service vs sidecar: choose a small horizontally-scalable centralized service behind the analytics gateway so we can manage cache consistency and publish invalidation events. Use a canonical predicate token (UUID) and push full predicate resolution to the gate; router uses the token to fetch predicate from cache or gate. For invalidation, rely on pub/sub (Kafka) to notify gate instances when role/dataset policies change. TTL default 30s with immediate invalidation on policy write.
tradeoffs:
- Performance vs staleness: shorter TTL reduces stale permission windows but increases cache miss rate. We opt for 30s + push invalidation to balance.
- Complexity vs latency: introducing a service adds network hop but reduces downstream DB lookups for common flows; we'll colocate gate in same AZs as gateway to keep p99 within SLO.
- Predicate token approach reduces serialized SQL in transit but requires an extra cache lookup when token isn't in router cache.
rollout_plan: 1) Feature-flagged dark launch: route 1% of analytics requests through gate and compare authorization latency and correctness. 2) Canary: 10% with extensive audit logging for 48h. 3) Gradual ramp to 100% by dataset and org size. 4) Emergency fallback: gateway can bypass gate and call legacy mapper if gate returns error. 5) Post-rollout monitoring for auth errors, cache miss rate, added latency.
acceptance_criteria:
- Unit and integration tests for gate logic and cache invalidation.
- End-to-end authorization correctness tests using sample polices and datasets.
- Median added latency at analytics gateway <= 8ms, p95 <= 35ms for common queries on canary traffic.
- Audit events emitted for every decision and surface in audit dashboard.
- No increase >0.5% in dashboard error rate during canary stage.

implementation_notes:
- Cache key: sha256(principal_id + '::' + dataset_id + '::' + role_vector_version).
- Store resolved predicate as parameterized SQL fragment with canonical column names to avoid injection risk.
- Use HMAC token hashing with per-cluster key for audit_ref.
- Provide metrics: auth_decisions_total, cache_hits_total, cache_misses_total, invalidations_total, added_latency_ms.histogram.
qa_plan: Create synthetic orgs with mixed role delegation and run EWMA load to validate correctness. Synthetic datasets with row-level markers to assert visibility. Run canary for 72h and validate audit trail completeness and latency metrics.
risks_and_mitigations:
- Risk: stale cache allows revoked access for short windows. Mitigation: immediate push invalidation on policy change and short TTL.
- Risk: increased complexity causing operational burden. Mitigation: start with limited endpoints (usage/cost only) and iterate.
- Risk: predicate canonicalization edge cases. Mitigation: maintain unit tests that assert canonical form for each policy type.
